title: Whence, whither, before whom (Avot 3:1)
hookLine: Akavia: know where you came from, where you're going, and before whom you'll give account
tomorrow: why pray for the people in charge, even ones you argue with?

lines: AGREE, AND THE JOB IS YOURS.
TAKE THEM BACK, HEAD THE COURT.
cards: Agree with the room, and the job is yours. The deal turns up in plenty of shapes: drop the objection, laugh at the joke, sign off on the plan. The Mishnah tells of a sage who got the big version.

Akavia ben Mahalalel held four rulings the other sages rejected. So they made him an offer: take back those four, and we'll make you head of the court. One sentence, said out loud, and the top seat was his.
What did he say, and which three things was he looking at?

teach.h: BETTER A FOOL THAN WICKED ONE HOUR.
teach.b: He said no. Better to be called a fool all my days, he answered, than to be wicked for one hour before God. He didn't want anyone saying he'd changed his mind for a title.

Avot's third chapter opens with the same man's method: look at three things, and you won't fall into the hands of wrongdoing. Know where you came from, where you're going, and before whom you'll give account.
First, whence. Akavia's answer is blunt: from a drop. Nobody begins impressive.
Every person in every room started the same small way, and another mishnah says humanity began from one person so that no one could say, my father is greater than yours. Second, whither: to dust.
Not a threat; a measuring stick. Hold a title up against the end of a life and it shrinks to size. Third, before whom: before the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He.
That's the question Akavia was answering when he turned the seat down. And the story has a twist.

teach.h: WHENCE: FROM A DROP, LIKE EVERYONE.
teach.b: Dying, he told his son to drop those four rulings: you heard them from one person, me; the others heard theirs from many.

teach.h: WHITHER: A TITLE SHRINKS TO SIZE.
BEFORE WHOM: THE KING OF KINGS.
teach.b: His son asked him to put in a good word with his colleagues.
He wouldn't. Your own deeds, he said, will bring you near or keep you far.

how: Some Jewish communities read a chapter of Pirkei Avot on Shabbat afternoons in the spring and summer; Akavia's three questions open chapter three.

o: where you came from: the first of Akavia's questions
where you're headed after this life is over
a polite old word for whenever you like

games.q: Akavia's three, and his deal — tap the pairs.
p: where you came from: a drop
take back four rulings, head the court

s: Akavia's first question is meant to make you feel worthless
it keeps everyone the same size: every person began the same small way.
Akavia refused to take back his rulings, even for the top seat on the court
better a fool all my days, he said, than wicked for one hour before God.
on his deathbed, he told his son to keep his rulings too
he told him to go with the many; the son had heard the rulings from one person.

games.q: your manager hints that the team lead job is yours if you quietly drop an objection you still think is right. by Akavia's story, what weighs most?
o: who you'll answer to, more than who's in the room.
the title, since a leader can fix things later.
the majority, since Akavia told his son to follow it.
games.why: Akavia turned down the head of the court rather than be wicked for one hour before God. he did tell his son to go with the many, but never for a seat.

practice: Take a scrap of paper and write three words down the side: whence, whither, before whom. Next to each, write one honest phrase about something on your mind this week, a decision, an argument, a title you want.
Then rest your eyes on the page, and let the third line be the last thing you read.

wordCard.voice: Whence: where did you come from? Akavia's first question, the start of chapter three, and the one that keeps everyone the same size.

orig.note: Hebrew: from where did you come? Akavia's first question, Avot 3:1.

carryVoice: Your line: whence, whither, before whom. Three questions that once turned down a promotion. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 3:1 (Akavia ben Mahalalel: whence, whither, before whom)
Mishnah, Eduyot 5:6–7 (the offer to be head of the court; the deathbed instruction to his son)
Mishnah, Sanhedrin 4:5 (one person created, so no one can say my father is greater than yours)
